name: Inequity aversion
statement: People will pay to avoid unequal payoffs, turning down money rather than accept a split that leaves them far behind the person they are dealing with.
meaning: Three claims travel under this name and they need separating. The first is a behavioural regularity: responders in bargaining experiments turn down small offers, which costs them money. The second is a formal model of preference. Fehr and Schmidt write utility as material payoff minus a penalty for the gap between own and others' payoffs, weighting the case of falling behind more heavily than the case of getting ahead. They call it self-centred inequity aversion, meaning a person cares about the gap between themselves and others rather than about inequality among third parties. Bolton and Ockenfels published a related model a year later, built on a person's share of the total payoff rather than on pairwise gaps. The third claim is comparative: that other animals share the aversion and refuse a poor reward when a neighbour gets a better one for the same work. The three stand or fall separately, and the evidence for them is of different quality.

origin.who: Ernst Fehr and Klaus M. Schmidt
origin.note: Their paper is "A Theory of Fairness, Competition, and Cooperation", 114(3), 817-868. It supplied the name and the algebra, citing Adams among earlier writers on equity and citing Loewenstein, Thompson and Bazerman for the asymmetry between falling behind and getting ahead. It cites Bolton and Ockenfels as a 1997 working paper, and that model appeared in the American Economic Review in 2000, built on a subject's own pecuniary payoff and own relative payoff standing. The experimental base both were built on starts with Güth, Schmittberger and Schwarze's ultimatum game in 1982.

evidence: Oosterbeek, Sloof and van de Kuilen pooled 37 papers reporting 75 ultimatum-game results. Proposers offered 40% of the pie on average and 16% of offers were rejected, with the rejection rate lower for larger pies and for larger shares offered. Fehr and Schmidt did not estimate their parameters and say so: their 2010 reply states that they never claimed to have estimated preference parameters and never used the word calibration in the 1999 paper. Their Table III assumes a discrete distribution chosen to fit known ultimatum evidence, with an envy weight of 0 for 30% of subjects, 0.5 for 30%, 1 for 30% and 4 for 10%, and a guilt weight of 0 for 30%, 0.25 for 30% and 0.6 for 40%. An envy weight of 1 means giving up a dollar to cut the opponent's payoff by two. Henrich and colleagues took the game to 15 small-scale societies. Group mean offers ran from 26% to 58%, against the 40% to 50% typical of student samples, and modal offers from 15% to 50%. Machiguenga horticulturalists in Peru had a mean of 0.26 and modes at 0.15 and 0.25, and their responders rejected a single offer although more than 75% of offers were below 30% of the pie. Lamalera whalers in Indonesia had a mean of 0.57, and 63% of proposers split the pie evenly. Hadza foragers rejected 24% of all offers and nine of the 21 offers at or below 20%. The Au and Gnau of Papua New Guinea rejected offers above 50% about as often as offers below it. Brosnan and de Waal tested five adult female brown capuchins in 2003 across four conditions. Their tendency to trade a token for cucumber varied across those conditions at F(3,16) = 25.78, p < 0.001, and fell furthest when a partner got a grape for no effort at all.

examples.tag: The split that is turned down
examples.text: Two strangers are handed a hundred pounds to divide, and the one offered ten of it refuses, so that both walk away with nothing. The refusal costs him the ten he was offered, and what he buys with it is the closing of the gap between them.

examples.tag: The pay rise that stops being one
examples.text: An employee is pleased with her rise until she learns that a colleague doing the same job got twice as much, and she takes a worse-paid post elsewhere. Her own pay never changed. The money she gives up is the price of not sitting behind the colleague.

examples.tag: The second job with the same partner
examples.text: Two decorators split a fee and one finds the other kept the larger share, so he turns down the next job although the rate would suit him. Refusing costs him work he wants, and the thing he is avoiding is the gap rather than the amount.

replication.headline: People really do reject low offers, at 16% across 75 ultimatum results, while no inequity effect survives a meta-analysis of 23 animal studies.
replication.detail: The two literatures pull apart. On the human side Oosterbeek, Sloof and van de Kuilen report a 16% rejection rate across 75 results from 37 papers, and the behavioural pattern is not in dispute. On the animal side Ritov, Völter, Raihani and Engelmann asked the authors of 30 eligible publications for their primary data and received it for 23, covering 24 studies, one of which they dropped for having no effortful task. What they analysed is 23 studies, 302 subjects, 60,430 observations and 18 species. The coefficient for the inequity condition was 0.257, with a bootstrapped 95% interval running from -0.029 to 0.543 and p = 0.0923. None of the five populations in their first model reached p < 0.05: capuchin monkeys gave 0.375 with an interval of -0.294 to 0.979, and chimpanzees gave -0.075 with an interval of -0.640 to 0.514. The disappointment condition, where a better reward is shown without a partner being favoured, gave 0.513 with an interval of 0.108 to 0.955 and p = 0.0339, and reached p < 0.05 in three of the five populations. A third model found no inequity effect left once disappointment was in it, at -0.001 with an interval of -0.392 to 0.347 across 17 studies and 244 subjects. Engelmann, Clift, Herrmann and Tomasello had shown the same thing directly in nine chimpanzees, who refused food from a human experimenter on 26.1% of trials and from a machine on 2.4%, and who refused most often when no partner was present at all.

study.cite: Ritov, O., Völter, C. J., Raihani, N. J., & Engelmann, J. M. (2024). No evidence for inequity aversion in non-human animals: a meta-analysis of accept/reject paradigms. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 291(2035), 20241452.

limits: The animal meta-analysis covers accept/reject tasks only. Its authors approached 30 eligible publications and received data for 23, and they dropped conditions in which the subject faced no effortful task, so the synthesis is narrower than the literature it reviews. The note to their Table 2 defines n as the number of species, while the column reads 302 for all species, which their text gives as the number of subjects. On the model side, Binmore and Shaked argue that ultimatum data cannot pin the Fehr-Schmidt parameters down at all: nothing more can be said of a proposer who offers half the pie than that the guilt weight exceeds 0.5, which makes the exercise a parametrisation rather than a calibration, and of the four games analysed in the 1999 paper they say only one arguably beats a money-maximising model. Fehr and Schmidt replied in the same issue that the criticism is unsubstantiated, while granting that a simple model may still be useful even though inequity aversion does not describe other-regarding preferences fully. Charness and Rabin ran distribution games built to separate the motives, and found few subjects would pay to reduce inequality by lowering another player's payoff. They observed Pareto-damaging behaviour more often when it increased inequality than when it reduced it, and they add that this comparison is itself confounded by other explanations. Dirk Engelmann and Martin Strobel ran 13 treatments in three classroom sessions at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, with 136 participants in 1998, 240 in 2000 and 210 in 2001. In their treatment P, where both fairness models predict the least efficient allocation, 60% of subjects took the efficient one. Their conditional logit gave odds ratios of 1.232 for efficiency at p = 0.012 and 1.492 for maximin at p < 0.001, while neither Fehr-Schmidt component was significant, at p = 0.161 and p = 0.286. Fehr, Naef and Schmidt re-ran two of those treatments on other subject pools and report that the efficiency result belongs to economics and business students: among Munich non-economists the egalitarian allocation was chosen by 57.8% and 54.2%, against 22.9% and 27.5% among Munich economists. Bolton and Ockenfels published a second comment in the same issue and Engelmann and Strobel replied to both; neither was obtained. Henrich and colleagues' own figures do not quite agree with each other: their text gives the range of group means as 26% to 58%, while their Table 2 lists Lamalera at 0.57 and Quichua at 0.25.
misreadings: Humans rejecting unfair offers, humans modelled as having inequity-averse preferences, and a monkey throwing cucumber are three claims, and evidence for one is not evidence for another. Henrich made the point in Nature: applied to the capuchin setup, the Fehr-Schmidt model predicts the monkey should eat the cucumber, because refusing it widens the gap rather than closing it, and the grape-receiving capuchin sometimes reached through the cage and took the discarded slice. Henrich also noted the human comparison. In an impunity game, where rejection costs the responder but leaves the proposer's payoff untouched, subjects never rejected. Wynne, reading Brosnan and de Waal's own data, reported 43% refusals in the inequality test against 49% in the food control, where a grape sat in the empty partner seat and no second monkey was present. Brosnan and de Waal answered that the levels are not the point and the trends differ. Their 2003 paper had tested the trend with an exact Wilcoxon that could not return a p below 0.06 on five subjects; the reply instead compares regression slopes across trials, at F(2,69) = 28.71, p < 0.001, which is a re-analysis rather than the printed test. Bräuer, Call and Tomasello tested 7 orangutans, 6 gorillas, 4 bonobos and 13 chimpanzees against the chimpanzee study Brosnan, Schiff and de Waal published in 2005, dropping the token exchange and adding a no-partner control. The apes ignored fewer food pieces when a conspecific received the better food, which is the opposite pattern, although across all four species that effect sits at F(1,29) = 4.19, p = 0.050, and is firmer in the chimpanzees alone at F(1,12) = 9.70, p = 0.009. They read it as expectation of food rather than as fairness. Roma and colleagues paired four capuchin models with four witnesses and found witness rejections infrequent and unrelated to what the model received, while models offered cucumber rejected it more often than witnesses did. Brosnan and de Waal answered that too, and Bräuer and colleagues describe their answer as a reanalysis of the original data that found no support for the frustration effect. The cross-cultural data also undercut the claim that everyone rejects unfair offers: Machiguenga responders rejected once, and the Kazakh, Quichua, Aché and Tsimane rejected nothing in 10, 14, 51 and 70 offers. The same ultimatum meta-analysis is used in the entries on reciprocity and two wrongs make a right, and the 15-society dataset also appears in the entry on cultural bias.
